n: Jesus gathers the Twelve and gives them both power (the ability) and authority (the right) to act in His name over evil spirits and disease. This is priesthood delegation in action.
Their mission mirrors His own: proclaim God’s kingdom and heal. Teaching and ministering to physical needs go hand in hand.

f.g: Greek apostellō, the root of “apostle” — one who is sent.

n: They are to travel light and trust God and the hospitality of others for their needs. The lesson is dependence on the Lord rather than on their own provisions.

f.g: Walking sticks.
A traveler’s bag for food and supplies.

n: Once welcomed into a home, they should stay there rather than shop around for better lodging. Contentment and loyalty to their hosts honors the work.

f.g: Stay.

n: Where people reject the message, the missionaries are to shake the dust off their feet — a symbolic act showing they have done their part and the responsibility now rests with the hearers.

f.w: shake off the very dust from your feet

n: The Twelve obey and go out, preaching the gospel and healing in village after village. Jesus’ ministry is multiplied through them.

f.g: Literally “announcing good news.”

n: News reaches Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. He is troubled because some say John the Baptist, whom he executed, has come back from the dead.

f.g: Ruler of a quarter — Herod Antipas governed Galilee and Perea under Rome after his father Herod the Great died.
Thoroughly puzzled and uneasy.

n: Others guess Jesus is Elijah returned, or another ancient prophet. Everyone senses He is someone extraordinary, but they cannot yet see who He truly is.

f.g: Greek form of the Hebrew name Elijah.

n: Herod’s guilty conscience speaks: he knows he killed John. His curiosity to see Jesus is finally satisfied at Jesus’ trial, but without faith.
The apostles return and report. Jesus takes them away to a quiet place near Bethsaida to rest — a reminder that even busy servants need time apart.

f.g: “House of fishing,” a town near where the Jordan enters the north end of the Sea of Galilee; home of Peter, Andrew, and Philip.
A lonely, uninhabited area, not necessarily sand dunes.

n: The crowds find them anyway. Instead of turning them away, Jesus welcomes them, teaches them, and heals those in need — compassion overriding His own need for rest.

f.g: He welcomed them warmly.

n: As evening approaches, the Twelve suggest sending the crowd off to find food and lodging. It seems the sensible thing to do in such a remote place.

f.g: Food, provisions.
Find a place to stay.

n: Jesus surprises them: “You feed them.” They can only count five loaves and two fish. He is teaching them to see what God can do with what little they have.

f.g: Food.

n: About five thousand men, plus women and children, are present. Jesus organizes them into groups of fifty, bringing order to the miracle.
The disciples follow His instructions and seat the crowd, acting in faith before they see how the food will appear.

f.g: Literally “recline,” the usual posture for a meal.

n: Jesus looks to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives the food to the disciples to distribute. These same actions will be repeated at the Last Supper, pointing to Him as the Bread of Life.
Everyone eats until satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers remain — more than they started with. God’s provision overflows.

f.g: Perhaps one for each apostle; the number twelve also recalls the tribes of Israel.

n: Luke, who often shows Jesus praying before key moments, places this question right after a time of prayer. Jesus asks what people are saying about Him.
The disciples report the popular opinions: John the Baptist, Elijah, or another prophet. People admire Him but miss His true identity.

f.g: Elijah.

n: Then Jesus makes it personal: “But who do you say I am?” Peter answers with a testimony: You are the Christ, the Anointed One sent by God.

f.g: Christ (Greek) and Messiah (Hebrew) both mean “Anointed One.”

n: Jesus tells them firmly not to spread this yet. Many expected a political Messiah, and He needed them first to understand what kind of Messiah He would be.

f.g: Strictly ordered.

n: Right after Peter’s confession, Jesus reveals that the Messiah must suffer, be rejected by the religious leaders, be killed, and rise on the third day. The Atonement is central to His mission.

f.g: Jesus’ favorite title for Himself; also echoing “Man of Holiness,” a name of God.

n: Discipleship means setting aside self-will and shouldering one’s own cross — every day. Luke’s word “daily” makes it a continual commitment, not a one-time act.

f.g: JST Matthew 16:26 adds that to take up one’s cross is to deny oneself of all ungodliness and worldly lust.

n: Here is the great paradox of the gospel: clutching our life for ourselves loses it, while giving it to Christ is how we truly find and keep it.

f.w: lose his life for my sake

n: Gaining everything the world offers is worthless if we lose our own souls in the process. Nothing is worth trading for eternal life.

f.g: Profited, benefited.

n: Anyone embarrassed to stand with Jesus and His teachings now will find Him unwilling to claim them when He returns in glory with His Father and the angels.
Jesus promises that some there will see God’s kingdom before they die. The Transfiguration, which follows immediately, is one fulfillment; Latter-day Saints also understand John’s promised tarrying.
About a week later Jesus takes Peter, John, and James up a mountain to pray. Mountains in scripture are often places of revelation.

f.g: Traditionally Mount Tabor; many scholars favor Mount Hermon near Caesarea Philippi.

n: While praying, Jesus is transfigured: His face changes and His clothes shine dazzling white, revealing the glory He had with the Father.

f.g: Gleaming, flashing like lightning.

f.w: the fashion of his countenance was altered

n: Moses and Elijah appear and talk with Him. Moses represents the law and Elijah the prophets — both bearing witness of Christ. Latter-day revelation teaches they also conferred priesthood keys on Peter, James, and John.
Only Luke records their topic: Jesus’ coming “decease” in Jerusalem. The glorious vision centers on His suffering and death.

f.g: Greek exodos, “departure” — echoing Israel’s Exodus; Jesus’ death would lead a new deliverance.

n: The three apostles were weighed down with sleep, but they fully awoke and saw His glory and the two heavenly visitors.
As Moses and Elijah begin to leave, Peter blurts out an offer to build three shelters, wanting to prolong the moment. Luke kindly notes he didn’t really know what he was saying.

f.g: Booths or tents, like those used at the Feast of Tabernacles.

n: A cloud overshadows them, like the cloud of God’s presence that led Israel and filled the tabernacle. The disciples are filled with awe as they enter it.
The Father speaks from the cloud, testifying that Jesus is His Son and commanding them to listen to Him — the Prophet greater than Moses.

f.w: This is my beloved Son: hear him

n: Suddenly only Jesus remains. The three keep what they saw to themselves, as Jesus had asked, until after the Resurrection.

f.g: Kept it secret.

n: The next day, coming down from the mountain, they meet a large crowd. Glory on the mountain gives way to human need in the valley.

f.g: The mountain of the Transfiguration.

n: A father shouts out a plea for his only child. Luke often notes when a child is an only child, highlighting a parent’s desperation.
The boy suffers violent seizures caused by an evil spirit: screaming, convulsing, foaming at the mouth, and being badly bruised.

f.g: Battering him severely; “hardly” means scarcely or with difficulty does it leave him.

n: The father reports that the disciples tried to cast it out but failed. Their earlier success had not yet taught them full dependence on God.
Jesus expresses grief at the unbelief around Him — among the crowd and even His disciples — then asks for the boy to be brought.

f.g: Twisted, turned away from what is right.
Put up with you.

n: Even as the boy approaches, the spirit throws him into a convulsion. Jesus rebukes it, heals the child, and gives him back to his father — a tender, restoring act.

f.g: Tore at him, threw him into convulsions.

n: Everyone marvels at God’s power. But amid the excitement, Jesus turns His disciples’ attention to something harder to accept.

f.g: Greek megaleiotēs, majesty or greatness.

n: He tells them to let these words sink in: He will be handed over to men. Popularity would not last; the cross was coming.

f.g: Handed over or betrayed.

n: They could not grasp it — the idea of a suffering Messiah did not fit their expectations — and they were afraid to ask Him about it.
Instead of understanding His humility, the disciples begin arguing about which of them is greatest — a painful contrast to His talk of suffering.

f.g: A dispute or debate.

n: Knowing their thoughts, Jesus places a little child next to Himself as a living lesson.

f.g: Next to Himself — a place of honor.

n: Welcoming the lowly — like a child, who had no status in that culture — is welcoming Christ and the Father. In His kingdom, greatness is measured by humility.

f.w: he that is least among you all, the same shall be great

n: John reports that they stopped someone casting out devils in Jesus’ name because he wasn’t part of their group.

f.g: Tried to stop.

n: Jesus tells them not to stop such people. Those doing good in His name are allies, not rivals. He rebukes a narrow, competitive spirit.

f.w: he that is not against us is for us

n: This marks a turning point in Luke. Knowing His time to be “received up” is near, Jesus resolutely heads for Jerusalem and the cross. Much of Luke 9–19 takes place on this journey.

f.g: Taken up — referring to His death, resurrection, and ascension.

n: He sends messengers ahead to arrange lodging in a Samaritan village along the way.

f.g: People of mixed Israelite heritage in central Palestine; Jews and Samaritans disagreed sharply over where to worship.

n: The Samaritans refuse to host Him because He is heading to Jerusalem, the rival worship center to their own Mount Gerizim.

f.w: his face was as though he would go to Jerusalem
f.g: He was clearly traveling toward Jerusalem.

n: James and John offer to call down fire like Elijah did. Their zeal is real, but their spirit is wrong — perhaps one reason Jesus called them “sons of thunder.”
Jesus turns and rebukes them. They don’t yet understand the spirit of His gospel, which is love, not vengeance.

f.w: Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of
f.g: Not in all ancient manuscripts, but fits Jesus’ teaching.

n: The Son of Man came to save lives, not destroy them. They simply move on to another village — answering rejection with patience.

f.w: not come to destroy men's lives, but to save them

n: On the road, a man enthusiastically promises to follow Jesus anywhere.

f.g: Wherever.

n: Jesus warns him to count the cost: even animals have homes, but He has none. Following Him means giving up comfort and security.

f.w: the Son of man hath not where to lay his head

n: Jesus invites another man, who asks to first bury his father. In that culture this might mean waiting until his father died, possibly years away.

f.g: Allow me.

n: Jesus’ startling answer: let the spiritually dead take care of such matters. The call to preach God’s kingdom takes priority over every other duty.

f.w: Let the dead bury their dead
f.g: Those spiritually dead can handle ordinary affairs; the disciple has a living work to do.

n: A third person wants to say goodbye at home first. Elijah allowed Elisha this, but Jesus’ call is even more urgent.
A farmer who keeps looking backward while plowing cuts a crooked furrow. A disciple whose heart keeps drifting back to the old life isn’t ready for the kingdom.

f.g: Plow; a light plow guided with one hand required forward focus.
